chapter_theme: The poet's praise of the city of Podanam, the capital of the Surama country, as a serpent's-world rival, a lotus on the earth, a heaven come down, a city of drums, anklets, bees and plenty, ending with the introduction of its king Payapati, gentle to those who approach and hot to foes.

cast.role: the king of the city of Podanam

36.reading: The city called Podanam stands inside a golden wall on the throne-ground of the Surama country, a fine town that seems to laugh at the world of the serpents.
36.nuance: Line 1 is a loose construction (the land's fame and the capital seated in it); the sense is the praise of the country before the city, and the comparison is with the Naga world below.

37.reading: The sea is a pond and the wide earth a lotus in it; in the lotus's honeyed centre lives red-eyed Tirumal in Surama, and the city takes the beauty of women's forms.
37.nuance: The poet builds the comparison in three nested steps (sea as pond, earth as lotus, Surama as its seed-vessel), and the last line turns the city into a woman's body, the poem's usual measure of beauty.

38.reading: The city's sky-reaching mansions, where the sun's horses graze and the clouds are caught on the frontage, seem a flower opened by the sea and set on the altar of the great ocean.
38.nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe; the image of the city as a flower laid on the ocean's altar rests on line 4.

39.reading: Beyond the groves, elephants chained at the roots of mango trees are fed sugar-cane, and bees drink pollen from the buds, all around the city's walled dwellings.

40.reading: The mansions rise like a jewelled mountain, where women with rain-dark painted eyes and lords in honeyed garlands play, and the creeper of desire is mixed with the wishing tree.
40.nuance: The mansion's pleasure is shown as love meeting wealth, with the creeper and the wishing tree the poet's own figures for desire and its fulfilment.

41.reading: The mansions are said to rival the mountains: incense smoke is the cloud, drums rumble like thunder, and women like banners show up like lightning.
41.nuance: Each part of the mansion has a mountain's counterpart (smoke-cloud, drum-thunder, banner-lightning); the poet is showing the whole built city as a weather.

42.reading: The golden halls, the silver bamboo-like pillars and the jewelled floors that gleam under the moon are said not to be made of earth.
42.nuance: The closing claim that the mansions are not earthen is praise by exaggeration, not a doctrine about the city.

43.reading: The jewelled drums, the anklets of dancing women and the songs of singers, all heard from the mansions, make the city sound like a hall of many instruments.

44.reading: The bees, drawn by the water-lilies and by the women's long eyes, mistake the eyes for flowers and, bewildered, grow weary buzzing among the dwellings.
44.nuance: The mistake of bees for flowers is the poet's stock image for the women's eyes, and the verse is praise of their beauty, not a scene.

45.reading: The crystal-slabbed benches along the shop-lined streets, with swaying garlands and bees, look like a grove of wishing trees.

46.reading: The sound of anklets of dark-eyed women echoing in the mansions makes the swans in the ponds restlessly wonder whether their mates have left them.
46.nuance: The swans' fear of parting is the poet's own touch, an image of separation set inside a description of plenty.

47.reading: The royal streets, stained with the red lac that women's anklet-sounding feet leave, look like lotuses blooming in a field.

48.reading: Lotuses, pearl strings that gleam like moonlight and jasmine garlands are not rare in the great city, so the speaker says there is no scarcity of such adornments.
48.nuance: The verse closes on the negative (not rare), so the sense is that adornments are plentiful; line 4 is short of a clear subject.

49.reading: The city's white mansions overflow with ripe fruits, the sweet water of three kinds, jackfruit, mango heaps and honey, as if the whole place were ripened.

50.reading: Its men and women, caught up in joy, know no difference between evening and morning, so that the golden city seems an Indra's heaven come down to earth.
50.nuance: The unawareness of time is praise of the city's pleasure; it contrasts with the Jain teaching of impermanence that the epic later brings in, but this verse does not make that contrast.

51.reading: The king of that great city, the single protector of the world under one white parasol, is the crowned, victorious king of kings called Payapati.
51.nuance: Line 2 is the common figure of a single parasol shading the world; the verse names the king only here, so who he is must come from the lines that follow.
51.event: Payapati, the city's king, is named and praised as sole protector under the white parasol.

52.reading: He is a king beyond reckoning in his works, whose command holds even the distant, gentle to those who come near and hot to enemies, with a great army.
52.nuance: The king is described as cool to those who come to him and fierce to foes, a double character that the praise treats as kingly, not as a flaw.

links.note: Verse 36 measures the city against the serpents' world below, and verse 50 against Indra's heaven above.
links.teaches: The poet bounds the city between the Naga world beneath and Indra's world above, so its praise is a scale with two ends, not one comparison repeated.

links.note: Verse 37 makes the city a woman's body and verse 46 fills its ponds with swans that hear her anklets and fear their mates are gone.
links.teaches: The poet moves from city as woman to a woman's sound as the cause of the birds' fear, so the beauty praised is also felt as loss, which verse 37 does not show.

links.note: Verse 40 gives the women's eyes rain-dark paint and the wishing tree, and verse 44 shows bees fooled by the same eyes into taking them for flowers.
links.teaches: The women's eyes are praised once by their effect on lords and once by their effect on bees, so the poet treats the same beauty as ruling men and nature alike.

links.note: Verse 52 gives Payapati a gentle face for those who come near; Kural 386 says a king easy to see and gentle in speech is praised above others.
links.teaches: The epic's king is gentle only to those who draw near and hot to foes, so the Kural's single ideal is shown split in two by the king's own enemies.

gains.a: The verse gains a standard that says why being easy to approach counts as praise in a king, which the city-description leaves unstated.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who keeps his gentleness for friends and is hot to foes, a limit on a rule the couplet states without exception.

source_issues: Verse 36 line 3: a stray space before a dead consonant was repaired by the build.
Verse 38 line 3 has a stray comma inside a word; the sense of lines 1-3 is not fixed.
